frames.narration: The browser connects to https://shop.example and starts a TLS handshake. It lists the protocol versions and ciphers it supports.
The server picks the settings and sends its certificate, which says: this public key belongs to shop.example, signed by a certificate authority.
The browser checks the certificate against the CAs it already trusts. It must be signed by one of them, unexpired, not revoked, and for exactly shop.example.
The checks pass. Now the two sides exchange key shares and each computes the same secret. The secret itself never crosses the network, so an eavesdropper cannot learn it.
The handshake is done. Every request and response is now encrypted with a fast symmetric cipher and carries an integrity tag.
Someone on the café Wi-Fi sees only scrambled bytes. If they change any of them, the integrity check fails and the connection is dropped.
Had an impostor answered instead, its certificate could not be valid for shop.example, so the browser would show a warning and stop. That is the authentication half of TLS.
